utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And meanwhile I'll deal with, to start with, two matters. The first, scheduling. Mr. Groome, you have made a suggestion by e-mail, that is, that Mr. Harland returns before he finishes his examination -- concludes his examination -- concludes now, in view of a possible re-call in the future. The Chamber does not agree with you and the Chamber would like to -- most likely will not be able to conclude Mr. Harland's testimony today. It would be preferred by the Chamber then to finish it tomorrow morning. We may even have some time between 9.00 and 10.30 before the next witness arrives and that might be the time we need. And that brings me to my -- of course we have to check, but we expect Mr. Harland to be available until he concludes his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has carefully considered the way in which you conducted your cross-examination and the Chamber has considered what was in dispute, what was most likely not in dispute, that could be reasonably expected to be in dispute. The Chamber has considered relevance. The Chamber has considered the way in which you sometimes elicited opinion evidence without focusing on the facts first. Taken all together, the Chamber considers that you have -- has decided that you have today to conclude your cross-examination, so you should finish your cross-examination today. That is our ruling. I see Mr. Harland has arrived in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd further like to inform you that a suggestion which was raised by Mr. Groome, that is, that you could conclude today and then perhaps later return, that the Chamber does not agree with that and that the Chamber would prefer you to conclude your examination, most likely not today but then tomorrow morning most likely. We even had considered to make an extended session today, but unfortunately due to the agendas of the Judges that's not impossible. Just to let you know we would like to accommodate you to returning to your place of origin today. But I don't know what you have discussed with Mr. Groome in this respect about availability. Mr. Groome, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think the Chamber misapprehends my application. Mr. Harland hasn't asked for anything. It was simply to ensure that General Dannatt was able to commence his testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you are playing an unknown role in a discussion about scheduling, but we expect that your examination and re-examination can be concluded tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, if you're ready please proceed. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you open paragraph 102 in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can somebody provide the statement to Mr. Harland, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're in April 1994 as we deal with paragraph 102 of your statement, and you say the year before Gorazde, together with Srebrenica, Zepa, and other areas, had been declared a safe area. By April the attack was underway. UNPROFOR was intensely involved in related cease-fire negotiations. You, yourself, mentioned the demilitarisation agreement from the 8th of May, 1993, in relation to Srebrenica and Zepa. Let me just ask you this: Yesterday you expressed some doubts in terms of whether UNPROFOR was supposed to deal with disarmament or not. In Article 3 of this agreement that was signed by General Ratko Mladic and Sefer Halilovic, his counterpart, in Article 3 it says: [In English] "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit over their weapons, ammunitions, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones and will be handed over to UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Article 5 says: [In English] "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone except members of UNPROFOR are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition, and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Can you tell me today how much was done on the basis of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's a confusion. I think - I'm not sure 20 years later - but I think you are quoting from the Srebrenica demilitarisation agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But here we raised the subject of Gorazde. I think Gorazde was not at that time covered by an agreement like that. So in Gorazde no action, not even a protest, would take place by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Srebrenica the presence of forces would be protested and the Bosnians had given a small amount of weapons, about 300 I think, which were generally very poor weapons and they had held onto the majority of weapons and they kept them deployed on the confrontation lines. But that was separate from different legal regime from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since Gorazde had a different legal regime, as you said, nevertheless, it still had been declared a safe area. Was it believed that international instruments for safe areas were supposed to be applied in relation to Gorazde as well as far as demilitarisation was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not -- it's not my recollection that the Security Council required a demilitarisation of any of the safe areas. The only reason the subject came up with Srebrenica and Zepa is because there was -- independent of the Security Council Resolution, there was an agreement between the parties, between Mladic and Halilovic witnessed by Valgren, I think the same one that you quoted, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that as far as the defence of Gorazde was concerned in April of 1994, NATO air force was used against Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not very successfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any dispute, Mr. Groome, about whether NATO air force was used against Serb positions in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who asked for the use of NATO air force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two separate ways of using NATO air attacks by UNPROFOR, the so-called close air support and the so-called air-strikes. If I remember correctly, these very minor air attacks in 1994 were under the close air support regime. So that would have meant that there was a request from a unit, an UNPROFOR unit, under attack, which would have sought authority from General Rose, who would have needed Mr. Akashi, the SRSG, and then it would have been authorised. It was a simpler, shorter mechanism for the close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that General Rose had asked on three other occasions to have NATO air force used again, but that Mr. Akashi refused that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Rose was, in general, not in favour of the use of air power against the Bosnian Serb forces, and he in fact raised the possibility of the use of NATO air attacks against the other parties. But it's possible that if there had been some particularly direct incident where he needed to extract his forces that he might have requested and it might have been rejected by Akashi. I have to say I can't remember at this distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 65 ter -- [In English] It's actually 1D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your report dated the 16th of April, 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2, paragraph 3 from the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what it says: "BH Commander Rose made three requests for close air support but these were rejected by the special representative of the Secretary-General, Akashi, who was in Pale at the time negotiating with the Serb leadership when the big Serb advance or offensive occurred." Do you remember now that this is what you had reported.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at this meeting. I believe that what happened is we were coming up as a delegation together from Sarajevo when the incident -- an incident took place in -- or near Gorazde, which in fact I think involved some of General Rose's special forces, the so-called joint commission officers, near Gorazde. He thought that air attacks might be necessary, so he returned to Sarajevo and I continued with Akashi to Pale. And I know that, in general, Mr. Akashi was reluctant to authorise the air attacks, and in this particular case felt that a cease-fire was within reach. Exactly what requests were made by whom, where, I don't know. But I do recall I think that the result was a NATO airplane got shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your memory serves you well. Would you agree with me that members of UNPROFOR provided information for NATO air-strikes, attacks?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's no need to tell the witness that what he said is correct or not; that is giving evidence rather than asking questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you think that because of providing information for NATO air-strikes, members of UNPROFOR sided with one side, thereby becoming a legitimate target themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that seems to ask for a legal conclusion about the status of UNPROFOR that I'm not sure Mr. Harland is qualified to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman already explained that they were concerned about it, had it in mind every time when they called for air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when they were concerned at the time, that is a fact, you are concerned or you are not. You can tell someone whether you are concerned or not. Whether now his opinion today is whether they -- from a legal point of view they were at risk by siding to become targets, that is a legal opinion you are seeking. If you would like to know of course you could ask the witness whether they considered at that time whether this would result in being targeted. There are other ways of finding the same information, but Mr. Groome is right, at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you are eliciting legal opinion. So please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rephrase your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks [Interpretation] Could we now have document 1D61 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this was sent as an order of the president of Republika Srpska, and it says in the first paragraph: [In English] "... will be received, an order from the president of Republika Srpska, highly confidential, number ... April the 20th, 1994, the title -- content of which is as follows ..." [Interpretation] And now we see that the president of the republic is issuing an order: [In English] "With reference to the complexity of the military/political situation and the urgency of achieving certain objectives and establishing an immediate influence" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we move on to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] "... of the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a little further down on the English version on the second page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My apologies to interrupt, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but we didn't have the right page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need the first page first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need the first page, but I think we asked for the first page but a little bit further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From number 1 [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then that was not visible on our screens a second ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And further, the president said: "... I have decided that, until further notice, the decision on the use of the Corps and other formations in combat can only be approved after I gave my approval to it." And then the paragraph number 2 on the second page: "I hereby forbid all levels of command to change the approved decisions on the use of units in combat activities without my approval." And under number 4: "I hereby forbid all levels of command to implement any amendments that approved decisions and issued orders without my approval."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were out in the field, did you see in practice that President Karadzic had operative command over the units of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. When we were in the field, the subordinate military officers would refer to the command of General Mladic. But when we were in Pale -- I think this was written, actually, on the 20th of April when we were also in Pale with Dr. Karadzic, I think our assessment was that there might have been some difference of view between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to paragraph 129. We need, in e-court that is, 65 ter number 10030.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an agreement on the elimination of sniper shooters in the Sarajevo area; right? [In English] "Recognising that civilians from all communities as well as UN personnel continue to be targets of sniper attacks in Sarajevo region." [Interpretation] This agreement did not establish whose troops were carrying out the attacks. The important thing was simply to stop the sniping; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, what was on our screen was the cover page, not the agreement itself. You quoted from which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we have the same -- now I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a -- it is a -- what is now on our screen is the cover page of a document which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I need the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- consists of four pages; and second page is a message; third page -- I think that in this document only on page 4 we find the agreement on elimination of sniping activities in Sarajevo region. There we have it. You were quoting from there, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting from the first page I have. It's actually -- probably what we have on our screen is the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what we have is the cover page of a four-page document where on the fourth page, and perhaps we could look at it at this very moment, that seems to be an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apparently this is -- was this uploaded by you or was it uploaded by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's also an associated exhibit to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Second page on the top most immediate. Yes, there we are. Mr. Lukic, please proceed. Is this what you needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we take a look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have page 2 on our screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then page 3. In English page 3 is paragraphs 4 and, surprisingly 6 instead of 5. Is this what you -- Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I suggest that you find it in the next break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now move to paragraph 135, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are in September 1994. Again, you say: "Karadzic began the meeting with an angry statement about the attack out of Sarajevo." This attack by Muslim forces came after UNPROFOR made the Serbs withdraw their weapons from the environs of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs hadn't withdrawn all of their weapons, but it was certainly long after the April ultimatum where they cantoned most of their weapons or moved them to other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harland. I thought I heard you say, and you are recorded as having said: The Serbs had not, "hadn't."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. They hadn't -- they had not removed -- they had not removed all of their weapons from the total exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you're not agreeing with the proposition put to you? The proposition put to you is that the Serbs had indeed removed their weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was agreeing with the proposition that it took place after the requirement that they do so, but I was objecting, as a matter of fact, as to whether they had fully done so. But the question was really about timing, right, and I agreed that it was after the April ultimatum and agreement, when, in theory, the sides were meant to have removed their heavy weapons or put them in collection points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I'm losing you. Because now you're putting your timing based on agreement; he's putting the timing based on actual activity on the ground. Did you -- did the attack place after the Serbs had already removed their weapons? That's the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my difficulty is that they partially removed their weapons in April and this event took place after that partial relocation of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This partial removal, was it largely removed? You say it was not fully. Do you have any information whether it was 10 per cent removed, 50 per cent removed, or more?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, the Serb and Bosnian sides were different because the Serb side, their heavy weapons were then in three categories. There were the category of weapons that were removed from the Sarajevo 20-kilometre zone in full compliance; there were the weapons that were placed into collection points within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone in compliance; and the weapons that were not in compliance that were left in combat positions within them. And if I remember correctly, the UNMO assessment of the time was that the majority of the heavy weapons were in the first two categories, so the -- they had more than 50 per cent complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that weaken Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I believe it probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time was the Muslim side asked to commit to anything or was it the case, as it usually was, that they were not required to do anything when that agreement was made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, "as it usually was" is comment and testimony rather than question. Could you answer the question, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were obligations that fell to the Bosnian side. They didn't have the option of removing weapons from the 20-kilometre zone because they couldn't get heavy weapons out of the city, but they were obliged also to put their weapons, heavy weapons, in a cantonment area and they -- like the Serbs, they partially complied. And I -- as with the Serb weapons collections points, I visited them. The main one was in Tito Barracks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view what was the purpose of weapon collection? Could it have been cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of a plan -- actually, I think a flawed plan, but an UNPROFOR plan of General Rose to try to bring about an end to the war by first almost imposing a cease-fire, and then using that cease-fire to allow for peace talks to take place. So, yes, it was part of a strategy, a campaign plan, but -- and ultimately unsuccessful [Realtime transcript read in error "successful"] one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you for a clarification. You said "ultimately unsuccessful" or "successful"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ultimately unsuccessful. I think that the view of many was that a sequenced approach, first a cease-fire then talks, would never produce a result because it would leave the Serbs controlling all of the land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was only for the record because it was recorded incorrectly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to move to paragraph 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're in October 1994. You say UNPROFOR had made plans to supply enclaves by force. What did that entail, briefly, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was first to seek the agreement of the Serbs to allow humanitarian aid through. If that did not succeed, to escalate one step which would be to force road convoys through or to drop humanitarian assistance from the air. And in a final stage, if those measures did not succeed, to use a major package of force, including helicopters, to attempt to resupply the three isolated eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although Gorazde, too, had been proclaimed a protected area, do you know that in the area surrounding Gorazde in the attacks launched by the fighters of the BH army, 60 villages were destroyed, Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was fighting in the vicinity of Gorazde at various points, but how many villages and at which points I can no longer precisely recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time did you deal with that? Did you write that in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 147, the next one, you again emphasise that there were restrictions on access to the enclaves for the UNPROFOR, and you say it was the policy of the Serbian military and political leadership. However, at the time, this same time, October 1994, NATO regularly struck Serb positions, both around Sarajevo and in other parts of Bosnia, such as Bihac and Gorazde. First of all, is this true? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regularly" is a big word. Maybe -- but on less than -- between maybe five and ten occasions there were air attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you believe today that those air-strikes, among other things, made the movement of convoys impossible? In other words, were convoys sent to areas that were subject to air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general the air attacks -- strictly speaking in UN terminology they were not air-strikes, they were close air support. Those air attacks would normally take place when a convoy was blocked or it was attacked. So the cause and effect are the other way around. UNPROFOR simply wanted to allow humanitarian assistance to reach the eastern enclaves and to fulfil its mandate to deter attacks on them. When the Serbs would either block the convoys or would attack the enclaves, then sometimes air power would be used against them, but it was that way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that NATO aircraft automatically fired rockets if Serbs turned on radars or fired at planes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was considered a hostile act under the terms of the Security Council Resolution declaring a no-fly zone over Bosnia and Herzegovina, over the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that also lead to the increased number of air attacks, NATO air attacks, on Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. And, in general, I can say that the policy of General Rose and Mr. Akashi were of maximum restraint in the use of air attacks. In my view at the time, in fact, they used them much less than the mandate of UNPROFOR might have indicated, and it was only during the later period under General Smith that a fuller [Realtime transcript read in error "full"] use of air attacks was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please could we move to paragraph 156 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Lukic. Did you say: "It was only in the later period under General Smith that a full" or "a fuller use of air attacks was used"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fuller, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fuller with e-r. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you say that the deputy commander of the Serb army, Milan Gvero, told General Rose that the Sarajevo airport cannot be reopened until Serbs receive written guarantees from the United Nations that NATO aircraft would not strike Serb targets without the approval of the Security Council. Is it true that at that time NATO aircraft were already attacking Serb positions without the approval of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The limited number of air attacks that took place did not require the authorisation of the Security Council, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who made that decision, the Security Council or NATO itself, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations Secretariat made an agreement with the NATO Secretariat on the arrangements that would govern it. So if I remember correctly, it -- Security Council Resolution 836 from 1993 authorises the use of all necessary means, including NATO air power, to -- in defence of the UNPROFOR mandate. And after that, the UN Secretariat and NATO Secretariat agreed on the so-called Blue Sword arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court 08163.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see the document. You mention it in this paragraph of your statement. You have reviewed the document, haven't you? It's your report dated 10 December 1994.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 2 -- sorry, page 3 reads: [In English] "By Saturday morning, all of the UNPROFOR detainees had been released, and some convoys were moving again, though there were still no fuel convoys. The airport remained closed." [Interpretation] We see that all members of the UNPROFOR were released. Is it the case that none of them had been hurt or killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph of your report, the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any dispute, Mr. Groome, about whether anyone was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it seems -- well, if I can point at many issues where it could be clearly expected that the matter is not in dispute, then I'm almost certain that you would be even better able to assess that. And I think if on a few of these items you've asked

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about that that no one was killed, you would have -- I mean, if Mr. Groome does not present such facts, then they are non-existent for the Chamber. If Mr. Groome doesn't say: And people were killed, then of course you would have to counter that if you disagree with him. But if Mr. Groome says people were detained and were released, then on the basis of such a presentation of facts this Chamber - and I think I'm speaking on behalf of my colleagues - would not out of the blue start to imagine that they may have been killed. So, please, could you keep this in the back of your mind as guidance for your cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your guidance, Your Honour, but this witness is one of a kind, so we have to elicit this information from him. If we miss this [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's no dispute about a fact, you don't have to elicit it from any witness. That's what my -- I tried to explain. If

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME SAYS
utterances.text: UN people were detained in February - I just give an example - that if he leaves it to that, you don't have to establish that they were not killed. If he doesn't say anymore, you don't have to establish that they were malnourished, you don't have to establish that they were -- that their uniforms were taken from them. If Mr. Groome establishes one fact, the Chamber will rely on that fact and will not start thinking what may have happened beyond of that. So you are countering matters which are not part of the Prosecution's case, are not in dispute. And that is if something is not in dispute, then of course the Chamber is not impressed very much by the results of the negotiations on agreed facts. But if you would have asked Mr. Groome: Is it the Prosecution's case or -- that those detained, that some of them were killed. And if he says no, then you could agree that those detained were released and that none of them were killed. It is not a matter in dispute. This Chamber would like to hear evidence focusing on matters where the parties disagree on factual issues. Would you -- you may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have to stress one thing. You know that we are rushed to this trial. We haven't seen all the evidence. We didn't have time to see all the statements, so I don't know what's coming in the future. If I have the witness which whom I can clarify one thing, I will clarify it. And as of today's date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I have the right to elicit the evidence the way I think is the most proper for my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this Chamber will keep in mind that if you are eliciting evidence on matters which could reasonably be expected not to be in dispute, you can verify that. You can ask Mr. Groome, as I did three, four, five times, no, no dispute about that. Then the Chamber will certainly consider this in the way in which it allows time for cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, could we now look at the last sentence in the next paragraph which says that US and French officials stressed, or rather, have noted that UNPROFOR's departure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what are you reading? What is the next paragraph? Next paragraph of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The statement we have already seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the next paragraph is deleted -- is redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, not from the statement, from this document we have on our screens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Starting with "many Serbs ..." but I'm interested in the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems that General Mladic is not feeling well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we should take a break and I think that the medical services should be called to assist. Can Mr. Mladic leave the courtroom or should he be treated? We adjourn - curtains please down - and the witness, Mr. Harland, could be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume the proceedings at this moment. Mr. Mladic has expressed concerns about his medical condition. He has been preliminarily seen by a nurse. A determination was made that he be further examined. The Chamber is unable to determine when Mr. Mladic will be able to attend court, and therefore the proceedings are adjourned for today. We will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 13th of July, and that we'll then either resume the cross-examination of you, Mr. Harland, or we'll further review the situation which then exists. Therefore, I'd like to instruct you, Mr. Harland, to - and I can imagine that it is a bit unexpected -- but that you not speak or communicate with anyone about your testimony either given or still to be given, and that you be back tomorrow at 9.00. The Registry is instructed to file confidentially a report on the results of the further examination, and if that could not be filed today then already sent as soon as it is available a courtesy copy to Chambers staff and to the parties. Mr. Groome, there's no need for the next witness to travel to be here tomorrow because his testimony would not start tomorrow anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. He'll appreciate being informed of that and I will do that as soon as we leave court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If there was any matter to be raised, it can be done now; otherwise, we will adjourn for the day. Nothing there. Then we adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 13th of July, at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of July, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.09 a.m.,
